summary: Specifies an experimental SMTP extension for sending and delivering messages that have internationalized email addresses or header information. It updates some syntax and rules in earlier email specifications, and relies on a separate document for communicating with systems that do not support it. It was replaced by RFC 6531.

eli5.summary: This lets the mail trucks carry letters whose addresses are written in any alphabet, not just plain English letters. It was an early trial version, replaced by RFC 6531.

subtitle: Sending email with addresses and text written in any alphabet.

tldr.problem: Traditional email systems limit addresses and headers to ASCII characters, making email inaccessible to people whose names or languages use other alphabets.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds a UTF8SMTP keyword to SMTP so mail servers and clients can send email with non-ASCII characters in the address envelope and headers, using UTF-8 encoding.
tldr.outcome: Internationalized email becomes possible, but servers must agree to support the extension; when they do not, messages can be downgraded to ASCII using an alternate address.

today: RFC 5336 is Experimental and was obsoleted by RFC 6531, which standardized and refined the SMTPUTF8 approach. Most modern email systems now support international addresses.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5336 defines SMTPUTF8, an SMTP extension that allows mail servers and clients to transport and deliver email messages containing internationalized email addresses and headers. The RFC tackles a fundamental problem: traditional email can only use ASCII characters (the English alphabet plus a few symbols), which excludes most of the world's writing systems.

The specification works by adding an optional service extension to SMTP—the protocol mail servers use to talk to each other. When a server announces support for UTF8SMTP, it signals that it can handle UTF-8 encoded addresses and headers. This is an experimental specification that was meant to explore how to make email truly international.
sections.eli5: Email was built when most computers were in English-speaking countries. SMTPUTF8 updates the mail-carrying protocol so addresses and messages can be written in any language.

sections.title: Internationalized Email Addresses
sections.content:
An internationalized email address has two parts: a local part (before the @ sign) and a domain part (after the @ sign). The RFC extends the syntax rules for both. The local part can now contain any UTF-8 character, and the domain part can contain UTF-8 characters as well, though domain names must also be processed according to the IDNA standard so they can work with DNS.

The grammar for internationalized mailbox names is formally defined using ABNF, replacing the ASCII-only productions from earlier RFCs. A quoted string in the local part can now include UTF-8 characters, and the domain labels can include Unicode. The key constraint is that mail servers relaying a message MUST NOT parse or transform the local part—they must treat it as opaque.
sections.eli5: An email address normally looks like smith@company.com. Now the part before the @ (smith) and the part after (company.com) can both have non-English letters.

sections.title: SMTP Extension Negotiation
sections.content:
When an SMTP client connects to a server, the server sends an EHLO greeting that lists its capabilities. If the server supports UTF8SMTP, it includes that keyword. The client can then use UTF-8 addresses in its MAIL and RCPT commands. If the server does not announce UTF8SMTP support, the client must choose one of four options: rewrite the message to ASCII (if it is a mail submission server), reject the message, find an alternate route, or downgrade the message using an alternate ASCII address.

The UTF8SMTP extension also adds an optional parameter called ALT-ADDRESS to the MAIL and RCPT commands. This parameter supplies an all-ASCII version of an internationalized address, allowing a message with UTF-8 addresses to be downgraded for delivery through servers that do not support the extension. The ALT-ADDRESS is only used when downgrading occurs.
sections.eli5: When a mail server connects to another server, they negotiate what features they both support. If both support SMTPUTF8, they can exchange addresses in any alphabet. If the receiving server does not support it, the sender can provide a backup ASCII address.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Downgrading
sections.content:
Since not all mail servers support UTF8SMTP, the RFC specifies how to handle internationalized messages when they encounter servers that do not. The extension requires that all servers supporting UTF8SMTP also support the 8BITMIME extension, which handles 8-bit data in message bodies. When a message with UTF-8 addresses encounters a non-UTF8SMTP server, several approaches are possible.

The most controlled approach is downgrading: converting the internationalized message to an all-ASCII form that uses the ALT-ADDRESS parameter if available. The specification also updates trace information (Received and Return-Path headers) to allow UTF-8 characters in certain places. Servers supporting UTF8SMTP can also send UTF-8 strings in responses to VRFY and EXPN commands if the client includes a UTF8REPLY parameter.
sections.eli5: Not every mail server in the world will update to support international addresses. So the system includes a fallback: if an international address is refused, the sender can try to resend it in plain ASCII using a backup address.

sections.title: Standards and Successors
sections.content:
RFC 5336 was published as an Experimental specification in September 2008. It updates earlier specifications (RFC 2821, RFC 2822, and RFC 4952) and is complemented by RFC 5335 on internationalized email headers and RFC 5337 on internationalized delivery status notifications. The extension defines new SMTP response codes and registers new IANA values for mail transmission types that combine UTF8SMTP with other extensions like STARTTLS and SMTP AUTH.

This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 6531 when the specification was revised and advanced to a higher standards track. The core concept of SMTPUTF8 proved successful and has been widely implemented in modern mail systems.
sections.eli5: This was a test version of the international email standard. It was replaced by RFC 6531, which refined the approach based on experience.
